title: The History of Dragon Quest | The RPG That Shaped Japan | Gaming History
description: The history of Dragon Quest: Yuji Horii, Akira Toriyama and Koichi Sugiyama, the 1986 Famicom original, the Slime, Dragon Quest III, the Square Enix era and Dragon Quest XI.

sections.heading: The RPG that shaped a genre
sections.script: Welcome back to the channel. Today we are looking at the history of Dragon Quest, one of the most important role playing game series ever made. In Japan, Dragon Quest is a national favorite, and the smiling blue Slime is as famous there as many film characters. Outside Japan, the series was first known as Dragon Warrior, and it took longer to reach a wide audience. But its influence is everywhere. Many role playing games that came later borrowed its simple menus, its clear goals and its sense of adventure. In this video, we will follow Dragon Quest from its start on a small home computer in the nineteen eighties to modern releases. Let us begin.

sections.heading: Three creators
sections.script: Dragon Quest was created by a trio. Yuji Horii wrote the scenario and designed the game. He had previously written The Portopia Serial Murder Case, often cited as the first visual novel. Akira Toriyama, the manga artist known for Dr. Slump and Dragon Ball, drew the characters and the monsters. Koichi Sugiyama, a classically trained composer, wrote the music, and he was reportedly the first composer to record video game music with a live orchestra. The game was made at Enix. This mix of a game writer, a famous manga artist and an orchestral composer gave the series a very clear identity from the start, and the identity never really changed.

sections.heading: The first game in 1986
sections.script: The first Dragon Quest was released in Japan in nineteen eighty six, on the Nintendo Famicom, published by Enix. According to Game Developer, it mixed the overhead exploration of Ultima with the first person random battles of Wizardry, and in doing so it effectively created the Japanese role playing game style. Horii wanted a game that beginners could understand without a thick manual. You walk across the map, talk to people, fight simple monsters and slowly grow stronger. Enix even moved the release to a Saturday instead of the usual Thursday, so children would not skip school to buy it. It was simple, but the formula worked, and a series was born.

sections.heading: Dragon Quest II and III
sections.script: Dragon Quest two followed in nineteen eighty seven in Japan, adding a party of heroes and a bigger world. Then came Dragon Quest three in nineteen eighty eight, which was the first real breakout hit and set sales records in Japan. It told the story of a hero who travels the world, and it let players choose their party members and their jobs. The game is remembered by many fans as a high point, and its release became a social event. Meanwhile, the first game came to North America in nineteen eighty nine as Dragon Warrior, published by Nintendo of America. The second reached North America in nineteen ninety, and the third in nineteen ninety two.

sections.heading: The Slime and the monsters
sections.script: No Dragon Quest story is complete without the Slime. It is a smiling drop of goo, usually the first enemy players meet and the weakest in the game. Akira Toriyama's design was so charming that it became the face of the series, and many variants followed, such as the King Slime and the Metal Slime. The monsters in Dragon Quest were not just enemies. They were also friendly, funny and full of character. That idea led to spin offs where players recruit monsters to their team, such as Dragon Quest Monsters, which was released in the United States as Dragon Warrior Monsters. Fans around the world know the Slime even if they have never played the main games.

sections.heading: Super Famicom and PlayStation
sections.script: The series kept growing with each generation. Dragon Quest five launched on the Super Famicom in nineteen ninety two, followed by Dragon Quest six in nineteen ninety five. Dragon Quest seven arrived on the PlayStation in two thousand in Japan and in two thousand one in North America. It reached multi-million sales in Japan, but it was largely ignored in America at the time, according to Game Developer. The pattern was clear. Dragon Quest was a mega hit at home, while the West needed more time. Each new game added bigger stories, richer worlds and new ways to play, while keeping the same comfortable turn-based style that fans loved.

sections.heading: Square Enix and Dragon Quest VIII
sections.script: In two thousand three, Square and Enix merged to become Square Enix, and Dragon Quest games began reaching more markets. Dragon Quest eight was released in Japan in two thousand four and in North America in two thousand five. It used a beautiful cel-shaded look and a full three dimensional world, and it sold much better in America than earlier entries, though still far below its Japanese numbers. It was also the first Dragon Quest to be released outside Japan under the Dragon Quest name. In two thousand nine Dragon Quest nine arrived on the Nintendo DS, the only main game first released on that system, and it was known for its multiplayer features.

sections.heading: Builders and new ideas
sections.script: The series also experimented with new styles. Dragon Quest Builders, released for the PlayStation four in twenty sixteen, mixed the world of Dragon Quest with a building and crafting game, and a sequel followed in July twenty nineteen on the Switch and PlayStation four. Spin offs such as Dragon Quest Monsters Joker brought monster collecting to more players, and its sequel reached North America in September twenty eleven. These games proved that the series was more than one formula. The charm of the monsters, the music and the humor could fit into different genres. For many players outside Japan, these spin offs were the doorway into the world of Dragon Quest.

sections.heading: Dragon Quest XI and farewells
sections.script: Dragon Quest eleven launched in Japan on July twenty ninth, twenty seventeen, and reached the rest of the world on September fourth, twenty eighteen. It was widely praised for its story, its colorful art and its respect for the series' roots. Sadly, the series also said goodbye to people. Koichi Sugiyama, the longtime composer, died in twenty twenty one at the age of ninety, and Akira Toriyama has also passed away. Their work remains part of every game. Yuji Horii remains the creative lead of the series, which shows how long this adventure has continued.

sections.heading: Music and memorable worlds
sections.script: Another reason Dragon Quest feels so special is its music. Koichi Sugiyama wrote the overture that fans in Japan know almost like a national anthem, and the orchestral recordings made the games feel grand even on early hardware. Add Akira Toriyama's friendly art, Yuji Horii's warm storytelling and the comfortable turn-based battles, and you get a series that welcomes everyone. Players of every age have grown up with its heroes, its towns and its quiet moments by the campfire. The series keeps proving that a game does not need to be complicated to be unforgettable. It only needs heart, charm and a good adventure to share.

sections.heading: A legacy of adventure
sections.script: Dragon Quest has now lasted for decades, and it still follows the same promise as the first game: a simple hero, a big world and a journey that anyone can enjoy. It shaped how role playing games were made, especially in Japan, and its music and monsters are loved by millions. Now we want to hear from you. Which Dragon Quest game is your favorite, and do you have a favorite Slime? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to the channel for more gaming history videos. Thanks for watching, and we will see you in the next one.

joke: The Slime is the weakest monster in the game, yet somehow it has the best fan club.
